rs12.argument: A reader might take 'Frost' and the winter evening as bracing, but 'spectre-gray', 'dregs', 'desolate' and 'weakening eye of day' are all images of decay. 'Invigorating' contradicts the stanza.
rs12.stem_issue: The quoted text is missing. The stem shows '(line 2)' and '(line 4)' instead of the actual phrases ('When Frost was spectre-gray', 'The weakening eye of day').

rs12.argument: Wind does blow through the stems, and line 12 later calls the wind a 'death-lament', so a reader could hear the stems as being played. But the strings belong to 'broken lyres', which can make no melody, and line 6 says nothing about sound.
rs12.stem_issue: The quotation for line 6 ('Like strings from broken lyres') is left out of the stem.

rs12.argument: 'The land's sharp features' does refer to the visible terrain, and 'cloudy canopy' to the sky. But the stem asks what the metaphor is for, and the key's answer, a funeral for the dead century, is the point. Literal description misses that.
rs12.stem_issue: The quotations are missing, which leaves the stem ungrammatical: 'a corpse with (line 11) and (line 12)'.

rs12.argument: 'I leant upon a coppice gate' puts him outdoors, and 'Had sought their household fires' puts everyone else inside. None of the other options fits the text.
rs12.stem_issue: The quoted text for lines 1 and 8 is missing.

rs12.argument: 'Seemed fervourless as I' measures the world against himself, which rules out the 'uniquely joyful' option (3). Nothing in the line mocks anyone.
rs12.stem_issue: The quotation for line 16 is missing.

rs12.argument: 'At once a voice outburst' gives a song of 'joy illimited', which breaks into the deathly scene. It does the opposite of confirming the speaker's fervourlessness.
rs12.stem_issue: The quotation for line 17 is missing.

rs12.argument: The bird sings in a 'blast-beruffled plume', so a reader could call it hardy. But 'aged', 'frail', 'gaunt' and 'small' all stress weakness, not strength.
rs12.stem_issue: The quotations for lines 21–22 are missing.

rs12.argument: Taken literally, 'fling' is a physical motion. But the bird flings 'his soul', not his body, and 'Had chosen' points to a deliberate act of will.
rs12.stem_issue: The quotation for line 23 is missing.

rs12.argument: 'Shrunken hard and dry' is set against 'full-hearted evensong'. The other options misread the contrast.
rs12.stem_issue: The quotations for lines 14 and 19 are missing.

rs12.argument: The bird survives the blast, but the poem stresses its frailty, and the final contrast is about what each one knows ('he knew' / 'I was unaware'), not about strength.
rs12.stem_issue: The quotations for lines 21 and 32 are missing.

rs12.argument: 'whereof he knew' could be read as saying the bird really does know. But it sits inside 'I could think', which makes it a guess, and 'divine plan' overreads 'Hope'.
rs12.stem_issue: The quotation for line 29 is missing.

rs12.argument: The poem ends on 'he knew / And I was unaware' and does not resolve the gap. None of the other options holds up against the text.
rs12.stem_issue: The quotation for line 31 is missing.

rs12.argument: Only line 25 speaks to the lack of cause for song. The full point depends on lines 25–28 together ('Was written on terrestrial things'), but the line is still the best evidence.
Option 1 accurately describes the first half, but 'nothing but despair' ignores the thrush and the 'blessed Hope'.

rs13.argument: "gazed at one another" could be read loosely as residents watching neighbours, but "literally" spying overreads a personification of the houses themselves.
Leaving money to "institutions" rather than to the poor could be read as a pointed exposure. But the tone is deadpan, not "openly scornful," and nothing says he hoarded wealth.
rs13.key_flaw: The explanation says the will 'gently undercuts' the word charitable. Giving to institutions is still a kind of charity, so the irony is real but subtle and debatable; the explanation presents it with a little too much certainty.

rs13.argument: Of the three books, the Memoirs of Vidocq is the adventure story, so a reader might think the boy prefers adventure. But the text gives his reason as "because its leaves were yellow," not the plot.
No distractor fits: the text never shows fear, the coachman is incidental, and the lanes are "dark muddy" and the gardens smell of ashpits, which rules out a clean, safe place.
The "feeble lanterns" give option 1 some surface support, but the word "only" makes it wrong. Nothing supports foreshadowing or exposure.
"teased her before he obeyed" does suggest the brother is reluctant to go in. But the contrast in the stem points to the narrator's fixed gaze ("looking at her").
Hiding behind the blind so he "could not be seen" might suggest shame, but the text never mentions guilt.
No distractor is supported. The "heart leaped" line shows excitement, not boredom, and the girl's feelings are never given.
"foolish" is a judgment, but it falls on his own blood, not on the girl, and it is rueful, not bitter.
"Her image accompanied me even in places the most hostile to romance" plainly extends her influence. None of the other options fits.
"throng of foes" picks up the drunken men and jostling, but "mainly fear" ignores the sacred chalice.
"These noises converged in a single sensation" hints at sensory overload, but the admissions in question are about feeling, not hearing.
rs13.stem_issue: "strange prayers" is in line 72, not lines 73-74. The stem's line reference should read 72-74.

rs13.argument: Her "fingers running upon the wires" makes her the player, but nothing suggests she does it "deliberately"; she may not even notice him.
rs13.stem_issue: The simile runs across lines 79-80, but the stem cites only line 79. Minor.

rs13.argument: The priest's will gets real attention, but it fills one paragraph and cannot carry a thesis about the whole passage.
"litanies" is religious language, but it describes the shop-boys' cries, not the narrator's infatuation.

rs15.argument: Algernon does say 'sentiment is my forte,' so a reader could take him at his word as someone who puts feeling first. But 'any one can play accurately' is plainly self-flattering, and the comic frame ('I keep science for Life') rules out reading him as a serious artist.

Lane does make a general claim: 'I have often observed that in married households...' A literal reader might call this a sincere expert opinion. But it plainly sidesteps the question of who drank the champagne, so composure is the better reading.

Lane does reveal something personal, so 'confessional' has a thin case. But calling the marriage 'a misunderstanding between myself and a young person,' and then saying 'I never think of it myself,' is flat understatement, not earnest confession.

Algernon complains that the lower orders have 'absolutely no sense of moral responsibility,' which sounds like moral worry. But his plan to 'forget the fact' of his own marriage shows the worry is not sincere and does not extend to his own class.

Someone might think Jack goes openly by two names. But Algernon calls him only 'Ernest,' and nothing on stage admits to a second name, so 'openly' is wrong. The gap exists only for the reader, which supports the key.
rs15.stem_issue: The question depends on speech labels that only a reader sees. The stem handles this properly by talking about the 'labeling' of lines.

rs15.argument: No other option fits. Jack never quarrels with his neighbours ('Never speak to one of them'). Algernon shows no resentment about Jack being away. Jack's mind is already made up ('expressly to propose').
rs15.key_flaw: Calling the reply a 'stammer' is a slight overstatement. 'Eh? Shropshire? Yes, of course' shows hesitation, then Jack quickly changes the subject. The reading itself is sound.

rs15.argument: 'One so young' does mention youth, but it refers to Algernon, not Jack. So the option misreads who is being described.
rs15.key_flaw: 'Preacherly' slightly overstates the language, but the mock-grave point holds.

rs15.argument: No rival works. Aunt Augusta's visit was announced earlier, at line 71. There is no engagement yet, and Algernon is mocking Jack, not approving of him.
Algernon says outright 'It is very romantic to be in love,' so option 0 contradicts the text.
Nothing in the text points to poverty, a secret acceptance, or hope for a happy marriage. Algernon goes on: 'I don't think you ever will be.'
Algernon does say the sandwiches are 'ordered specially for Aunt Augusta,' which could look like devotion to her. But he eats them himself, so the devotion is only a pretext.

Lane outwits Algernon, and Algernon's own line ('if the lower orders don't set us a good example') invites a reading that servants come off better. But Lane also drinks the champagne and dismisses his own marriage, so 'morally far superior' and 'faithfully' go too far.
rs15.key_flaw: The justification cites the sandwich double standard as evidence about 'pieties about marriage,' but the sandwiches are not about marriage. It also says each example is 'delivered through an inverted epigram,' which is not true of the sandwich business. That is stage action plus 'She is my aunt,' not an epigram. Also, some of the marriage inversions come from Lane, who is not upper-class, so 'upper-class pieties' only partly fits.
